canonical_statement: The review aims to summarize practical evidence on prevention, diagnosis, risk stratification, and management of pulmonary embolism in critically ill ICU patients, especially ICU-acquired PE.

Critically ill ICU patients are at increased thromboembolic risk because of factors including mechanical ventilation, prolonged immobilization, inflammation, infection, endothelial/coagulation dysfunction, central venous catheters, sedatives, paralytics, and vasopressors.
The review reports that post-mortem studies diagnose only about one-third of pulmonary emboli occurring in ICU patients.
The review reports a mechanically ventilated cohort in which protocolized CT imaging detected PE in 18.7% of patients and 60% of detected PE cases were clinically silent.
The review reports untreated pulmonary embolism mortality of approximately 30%, compared with 2-8% with anticoagulant therapy.
Pharmacologic thromboprophylaxis options in critically ill patients include UFH, LMWHs, and fondaparinux, with recent practice shifting toward LMWH use.
The review summarizes the PROTECT trial as showing fewer pulmonary emboli with LMWH than UFH in critically ill patients without increased bleeding complications or bleeding-related deaths.

canonical_statement: For high-risk groups such as trauma patients, the review notes that higher or intermediate prophylaxis doses, twice-daily dosing, and anti-Xa monitoring have been described or advised.
Active bleeding or high bleeding risk, particularly recent traumatic intracranial hemorrhage or hemorrhagic stroke, is presented as a contraindication to pharmacologic anticoagulant prophylaxis.
The review states that current recommendations support thromboprophylaxis when platelet count is above 50,000, while noting that supporting data are limited.
When platelet count is 20,000-50,000, the review states that prophylactic anticoagulation may be considered cautiously with close monitoring and individualized decision-making.

For ICU patients who cannot receive immediate pharmacologic prophylaxis, mechanical prophylaxis remains an option, with stronger support for intermittent pneumatic compression than graduated compression stockings.

HIT should be suspected when thrombocytopenia and/or thrombosis occur in temporal association with heparin after excluding other causes; laboratory detection of anti-PF4/heparin antibodies is required for confirmation.
When HIT is suspected, the review recommends stopping all heparin sources and starting a non-heparin parenteral agent; bivalirudin and argatroban are preferred options in critically ill patients.
The review states that HIT risk is lower with LMWH than UFH and lower still, but not zero, with fondaparinux.
Anti-Xa monitoring is presented as a strategy to reduce LMWH over- and under-dosing in critically ill patients, particularly when organ failure such as renal failure alters heparin pharmacokinetics.

For twice-daily prophylactic enoxaparin, the review reports an anti-Xa target of 0.2-0.4 IU/mL measured 3-4 hours after the last dose after at least three consecutive doses, while emphasizing assay- and agent-specific local protocols.
Persistent unexplained hypoxemia, unexplained tachycardia, and unexplained hypotension are described as the most common triggers for suspicion of PE in ICU patients.

Simplified Geneva and Wells prediction rules are useful in general populations but were not specifically designed for critically ill patients, and several component variables are confounded by critical illness.

Continuous ICU monitoring may raise suspicion for PE through right-ventricular strain ECG changes, new sinus tachycardia or atrial fibrillation, and hemodynamic patterns consistent with right-ventricular dysfunction, but these findings are not PE-specific.
The review reports a sensitivity of 83% for CT pulmonary angiography in diagnosing pulmonary embolism.

canonical_statement: CTPA is presented as the diagnostic test of choice for PE, but ICU use carries transport, radiation, contrast-reaction, and contrast-associated kidney-injury concerns that should not automatically preclude imaging when PE is suspected.

The review identifies the 60/60 sign and McConnell sign as relatively specific echocardiographic findings for PE, while noting that they are detected in fewer than 20% of unselected PE cases and their absence does not exclude PE.

In a patient with high clinical suspicion for PE, detection of lower-extremity DVT by compression ultrasound is described as a highly specific finding that can justify initiation of therapeutic measures.
Triple-POCUS combines cardiac, lung, and lower-extremity compression ultrasound; the review notes emergency-department evidence but no supportive evidence for its application in ICU patients.
D-dimer testing is described as less useful and not recommended for diagnosing PE in ICU patients because many ICU conditions elevate D-dimer and erode specificity.

PE risk stratification in the ICU is challenging because respiratory failure, hemodynamic instability, right-ventricular dysfunction, and biomarker abnormalities may arise from critical illness rather than PE.

Table 3 notes that more than 50% of critically ill patients may be receiving vasopressors, more than 25% may have non-ARDS hypoxemia, and cardiac troponin elevation has been reported in more than 40% of critically ill populations, complicating PE risk stratification.
The review reports a 30-day mortality risk of 1.0% for patients with an sPESI score of 0.

canonical_statement: For PE risk stratification, hemodynamic instability is defined by cardiac arrest, systolic blood pressure below 90 mmHg, vasopressor requirement to maintain systolic pressure at least 90 mmHg despite adequate fluids, or a systolic pressure fall of 40 mmHg lasting more than 15 minutes.

outcome.definition: Cardiac arrest; SBP <90 mmHg; vasopressors needed to maintain SBP >=90 mmHg despite adequate fluid resuscitation; or SBP drop of 40 mmHg for >15 min.

canonical_statement: Cardiac troponin and other PE risk biomarkers are difficult to interpret in critically ill patients because sepsis, hypotension, arrhythmia, renal dysfunction, and other comorbidities can elevate them; no troponin threshold definitively attributes elevation to PE.

In PE with respiratory compromise, the review recommends correcting hypoxemia while minimizing positive ventilatory pressures and avoiding hypercapnia because these can worsen right-ventricular loading.

For hemodynamic support in PE, the review describes norepinephrine as the catecholamine of choice for arterial pressure and dobutamine below 10 micrograms/kg/min as the inotrope of choice for right-ventricular contractility, while discouraging aggressive fluid loading.

VA-ECMO is described as an adjunct to reperfusion for PE with refractory circulatory collapse or cardiac arrest and as possible salvage therapy when treatment fails or thrombolysis is contraindicated, but randomized efficacy and safety data are absent.

canonical_statement: The review aligns low- and intermediate-risk PE with therapeutic anticoagulation, high-risk PE with reperfusion treatment, and intermediate-high-risk PE with close monitoring and immediate reperfusion if clinical deterioration occurs.

Critically ill patients may have impaired subcutaneous absorption, reduced renal clearance, altered distribution after fluid resuscitation or vasopressors, and unexpected procedural needs, all of which can complicate LMWH use and bleeding risk.

For twice-daily therapeutic LMWH, the review reports a peak anti-Xa target of 0.5-1.2 IU/mL measured about 4 hours after administration, while advising use of agent- and laboratory-specific local guidance.

canonical_statement: Table 6 states that continuous UFH infusion should be adjusted toward an activated partial thromboplastin time of 1.5-2.3 times control.

Table 6 cautions that fondaparinux can increase bleeding risk with impaired creatinine clearance and advises anti-Xa monitoring if fondaparinux is necessary for HIT when preferred alternative agents are unavailable.
UFH may be preferred when hemorrhage risk is high because it can be stopped and rapidly reversed, and when hemodynamic deterioration may require reperfusion therapy.
When unusually high UFH doses are required to reach aPTT targets, the review notes that anti-factor Xa monitoring may prevent unnecessary escalation when heparin levels are otherwise adequate.

IVC filters may be considered for lower-extremity DVT with an absolute contraindication to therapeutic anticoagulation, recurrent PE despite adequate anticoagulation, or a necessary delay in anticoagulation, but routine IVC-filter use for PE prevention is not advised.

IVC filters should be removed as soon as they are no longer needed; reported complications include venous-wall penetration, filter embolization, thrombosis, and infection risk in critically ill patients.
Systemic thrombolysis is indicated for high-risk PE and selected intermediate-high-risk patients, but carries major bleeding and intracranial hemorrhage risk.

Absolute thrombolysis contraindications listed by the review include recent major surgery or trauma, active bleeding or bleeding diathesis, prior hemorrhagic stroke, ischemic stroke within six months, and central nervous system neoplasm.
For intermediate-high-risk PE, close observation is favored because guideline support for routine thrombolysis is lacking and bleeding risk may outweigh hemodynamic benefit.

canonical_statement: When systemic thrombolysis is contraindicated or fails, surgical embolectomy or catheter-directed therapies are alternatives, but randomized comparative data for surgery and adequately powered high-risk comparisons for catheter approaches are lacking.

The review concludes that anticoagulation in critically ill PE patients requires individualized management because bleeding risk, thrombocytopenia, renal impairment, altered volume of distribution, invasive-procedure needs, and thrombolysis contraindications complicate standard pathways.
The authors note that randomized controlled trials often exclude critically ill patients, increasing reliance on prospective observational data and case series for ICU PE management.
